messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Sok is a 72-year-old retired refugee aid worker who now lives quietly with his wife in a small apartment on the outskirts of a midwestern city. For decades he had worked in camps along the Thai–Cambodian border, helping families resettle after years of displacement. Then, during a distribution of supplies in a new camp, a suicide bomber detonated himself among the crowd. Sok was thrown against a concrete wall and lost consciousness; when he woke, the scene was scattered with bodies and the air was thick with dust and screams. He can still see the images—a child’s sandal, a torn blue tarpaulin, the spray of blood against white sacks of rice—and often, without warning, he hears the blast and the high-pitched ringing that followed, as if it is happening again in the room. Sometimes the memory feels so extreme that he has to remind himself it actually happened; the unreality of it makes him question his own mind.

Those vivid recollections pull him into a loop of self-blame that he cannot escape. When the images come, he finds himself rehearsing what he could have done differently—maybe he should have spotted the bomber, maybe he should have shouted, maybe he should have blocked the door. The rumination is relentless, and it has reshaped his daily life. He no longer drives or even rides as a passenger in a car, because the sounds of traffic—a horn, a backfire, a sudden thud—are too close to the explosion’s echo. He also avoids any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation. When his wife gently suggests he see a doctor, he agrees quickly just to end the conversation; the thought of an argument makes his chest tighten as if another blast is coming.

The auditory and visual memories also keep Sok in a constant state of hypervigilance. The moment he hears a sound that reminds him of the attack—a door slamming, a truck rumbling past, a child’s sharp cry—he jumps, his body already tensed for flight. He has become hyperalert in his own home, scanning the street outside the window, checking the lock on the front door several times a day. This watchfulness, in turn, seems to feed the memories: the more he scans for danger, the more the attack replays in his mind, as though his brain is trying to prove that the threat is still present. He only feels safe in a very limited number of places—his own living room, the neighborhood park before dawn when no one else is there, the corner of a coffee shop where his back is to a wall. Anywhere else, the startle reflex is so strong that a neighbor’s knock can send him gasping.

These patterns have been solidifying for months. At first, Sok told himself he was just being careful, that after such a long career he deserved to rest. But now his world has shrunk to a few safe zones, and his wife has begun to worry about his isolation. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last week when he heard the mail slot clatter and dropped to the floor, arms over his head, before he realized he was inside his own house. He is terrified that he is losing control of his mind, that the memories will eventually erase the life he built after the war. He wants to be able to sit in a car without flinching, to disagree with his wife without feeling he is about to die. But what frightens him most is the possibility that the therapy will ask him to go back into the memory he can barely believe is real.
